title: The Retention Agreement: Why Your Key People Have to Sign Before a Buyer Will Pay Full Price
excerpt: A retention agreement for your key staff isn't paperwork. It's where a buyer quietly prices owner dependence, and it can decide how much of your sale price you actually keep.
content:
The term sheet is signed, the data room is open, and the deal finally feels real. Then the buyer's lawyer sends through a short list of documents still needed before settlement, and near the bottom sits something most owners didn't expect: retention agreements for the operations manager, the senior estimator, and the longest-serving team member, each one asking that person to commit to staying for twelve to eighteen months after the sale.

It lands as an administrative step. It isn't. What the buyer is really doing is pricing the part of the business that doesn't belong to the owner, the part that lives in two or three people's relationships and know-how, and deciding how much of the purchase price should depend on those people actually turning up on day two of new ownership.

The owner who hasn't thought about this moment in advance usually finds out the hard way that the number on the term sheet and the number that eventually lands in the bank account are not quite the same figure.

Why a Buyer Asks for This at All

A buyer isn't paying for last year's profit and loss statement. They're paying for the expectation that the cash flow behind that P&L keeps showing up after settlement. If a meaningful share of revenue, client relationships or technical delivery sits with people other than the owner, the buyer has no way to verify that cash flow survives the handover unless those people are formally committed to stay. The retention agreement is how a buyer turns an assumption about the future into something closer to a guarantee, or at least something they can hold the deal to if it doesn't play out that way.

The Price Is Rarely Where You Think It Is

The detail most owners miss is where the retention cost actually sits. In a lot of deals it isn't a separate amount the buyer funds out of their own pocket. It's structured as a holdback against the purchase price, released only once the retention period is served, or folded into an earnout that pays out in stages tied to the same key people staying and performing. The headline figure in the letter of intent was never fully yours to bank on day one. How much of it you actually keep depends on whether the people the buyer is worried about losing agree to sign, and whether they stay the course once they have.

What the Request Is Actually Measuring

Strip the legal language away and a retention agreement is a direct measurement of owner and key-person dependence, the same dependence that shows up as a discount on the multiple long before any buyer sends a term sheet. A business that can genuinely run without its three most important people for eighteen months is a different asset to a buyer than one that can't, and the retention clause is simply where that difference becomes visible in dollar terms. This is exactly the dimension an Exit Readiness Diagnostic scores well before a sale process starts, because the pattern across owner-led businesses is that this gap is easier to see from the outside than from inside the day-to-day running of the business.

Building the Retention Story Before You're in Due Diligence

The owners who come through this moment cleanly are rarely the ones negotiating retention terms for the first time in due diligence. They're the ones who built incentive structures, defined career paths, and gave key people a real stake in the outcome years before a buyer ever appeared, so the eventual retention agreement reads as confirmation of an existing relationship rather than a new demand under pressure. That groundwork is also what protects the price itself. A key person who already expects to be asked usually signs without friction, where one who is hearing about the sale and the retention request in the same week has far more room to negotiate on their own terms, and far more reason to hesitate. The exit readiness guide on the ProfitPulse site walks through the other seven dimensions buyers assess alongside this one.

None of this means a sale has to run into the same surprise every time. Knowing where a business's dependence actually sits, and doing something about it years rather than months before a deal, is the difference between a retention agreement that simply confirms what everyone already expected and one that becomes a last-minute sticking point for someone else to exploit. If you're not sure how dependent your sale price currently is on a handful of people, an indicative business valuation is a useful place to start that conversation before a buyer starts it for you.

faqs.q: What is a retention agreement in an Australian business sale?
faqs.a: A retention agreement is a separate commitment, usually requested by the buyer's lawyers during due diligence, where a key staff member agrees to stay with the business for a set period after settlement, often twelve to eighteen months. It gives the buyer confidence that the relationships and knowledge the sale price depends on don't leave with the old ownership structure.

faqs.q: Why would a buyer hold back part of the purchase price for staff retention?
faqs.a: A buyer is paying for cash flow they expect to continue, not just the figure on last year's financials. If that cash flow depends heavily on one or two key people, holding back part of the price until those people have stayed and performed is how the buyer manages the risk that the business looks different without them. It's a pricing mechanism, not a sign of distrust in the owner.

faqs.q: Can a business sale fall through if key employees won't sign a retention agreement?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens more often than owners expect. If a key person won't commit, or the buyer senses genuine flight risk, the buyer will often reprice the deal, restructure it as an earnout, or walk away entirely. It's one of the reasons an Exit Readiness Diagnostic is worth running well before a sale process, so these conversations happen on your terms.

faqs.q: How does owner dependence affect the multiple I get for my business?
faqs.a: The pattern across owner-led businesses is that the more a business's results trace back to one or two individuals, the more a buyer discounts the multiple to account for that risk. Reducing that dependence before you're in a sale process, rather than promising to reduce it afterwards, is one of the more reliable ways to protect the number a business valuation ultimately lands on.

faqs.q: Should I tell key staff I'm planning to sell the business?
faqs.a: There's no single right answer, and it depends heavily on your relationship with that person and how far along the sale process is. What matters more than the timing of the conversation is whether the incentive and career structure around that person was already fair and clear before the question of a sale ever came up.

faqs.q: How can I reduce a business's dependence on key people before selling it?
faqs.a: The usual levers are documenting the knowledge and relationships that currently sit in someone's head, building a genuine second layer of leadership, and giving key people a real stake in the outcome well ahead of any sale conversation. The exit readiness guide covers this alongside the other readiness dimensions buyers assess.
